hints: Start with a rotation of the first permutation, so every position differs from its first forbidden value.
If a position still matches its second forbidden value, swap its entry with a carefully chosen other position.
At most four positions are unsuitable as swap partners, so checking five positions is enough when n>=5.
analogy: A misplaced value can be exchanged with another position as long as both values remain allowed after the exchange.
example: For a=[1,2,3] and b=[2,3,1], c=[3,1,2] differs from both arrays at every position.
algorithm: For n<=4 try every permutation and print a valid one or IMPOSSIBLE. For n>=5 initialize c[i]=a[(i+1) mod n]. Scan positions; whenever c[i] equals a[i] or b[i], find a position j among the first five such that c[j] differs from both a[i],b[i] and c[i] differs from both a[j],b[j]. Swap c[i] and c[j]. Output c.
correctness: Initially c is a permutation, and swaps preserve that. For a bad position i, at most two positions contain its forbidden values and at most two positions forbid c[i], since each forbidden array is a permutation. Thus among five positions at least one partner works. The swap fixes i and leaves j valid, so all processed positions stay valid. Exhaustive search handles the smaller cases.
complexity: For n elements, O(n) time and O(n) space; brute force uses at most 4! permutations.
